newsitem.title: ETHIOPIA: Ethiopia wants other candidates for top U.N. job.
newsitem.headline: Ethiopia wants other candidates for top U.N. job.

text.p: Ethiopia has urged Africa to abandon its support for embattled U.N. Secretary General Boutros Boutros-Ghali and called on the world's poorest continent to present alternative candidates for his job.
The call by Ethiopian Prime Minister Meles Zenawi came in a letter to Cameroon President Paul Biya who is chairman of the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) -- Africa's United Nations.
The letter, dated November 20 and obtained by Reuters on Tuesday, represents a break in African support for Boutros-Ghali's campaign to win another five-year term.

"It seems to me therefore it is now time for our permanent representative in New York and for all OAU member states in their individual capitals, to make it clear to our partners that Africa has other worthy personalities who should be considered for taking over as secretary-general of the United Nations," Meles said.

He added: "Africa deserves, merits a second term in that position. The necessary lobbying should and must start right away. Any further delay, I am seriously concerned, would result in a fatal blow to this African chance."
"...time is of essence now and it is my earnest hope that you would continue to provide the necessary leadership on this matter so that Africa would not lose this opportunity by default."
The United States used its veto last week while the other 14 U.N. Security Council members supported Boutros-Ghali, 74, whose term ends on December 31.

Meles said the spirit of the consensus reached at the OAU annual summit in Yaounde was to support the incumbent "as far as practicably possible and as long as doing so is deemed to produce the desired results".
He added that the consensus was not to circle the wagon "come what may".
It was the first sign there were serious cracks in Africa's position that the continent fully backed the Egyptian diplomat who is criticised by Washington for failing to reform the U.N..
Many African nations as well as France had apparently hoped that by not putting forward other candidates, the Council at minimum could negotiate a compromise for a two-year term.
"We don't have any (new) list. It is composed of one person, Dr. Boutros-Ghali," said Botswana's U.N. ambassador Legwaila Joseph Legwaila, after a council meeting on Monday.

The 15-seat Council, which casts the decisive vote, has agreed to give priority to candidates from Africa on the grounds that if Boutros-Ghali is denied the second term given his predecessors, he should at least be followed by another African.
Biya is expected to telephone heads of African nations this week, but no one expects a quick reply from 52 members before the Council meets on the subject again on Friday.

Meles' letter said: "...the mandate the (OAU) summit gave your excellency (was to) take the necessary steps with all partners, members of the U.N. to give Africa a second mandate for the next five years."

Among Africans mentioned as potential candidates are Under-Secretary-General Kofi Annan of Ghana, who heads U.N. peacekeeping operations; Amara Essy, foreign minister of the Ivory Coast and Hamid Algabid of Niger, secretary-general of the Organisation of the Islamic Conference.

Others are Salim Ahmed Salim of Tanzania, the secretary-general of the Organisation of African Unity and Olara Otunnu, a former Ugandan U.N. envoy who heads the New York-based International Peace Academy.
